summary: Extends EAP and its keying hierarchy to support the EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP), an efficient way to re-authenticate without repeating the whole EAP exchange when moving to another authenticator. It works independently of the EAP method used. It was replaced by RFC 6696.

eli5.summary: When you move between Wi-Fi access points, logging in again from scratch is slow. This lets you show a quick pass from your earlier login. It has been replaced by RFC 6696.

questions: how to speed up wifi roaming authentication
how does erp speed up wifi roaming
does erp protect against replay attacks
subtitle: Fast re-authentication for moving devices without repeating the full login.

tldr.problem: When a device moves between network access points, it must re-authenticate with the network. A full EAP authentication exchange can take several round trips and cause handover delays, and not all EAP methods support re-authentication.
tldr.mechanism: The EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP) allows a device to prove it holds key material from a previous full EAP authentication without repeating the entire exchange. It derives a re-authentication root key from the original keys and uses it for one-round-trip exchanges with a re-authentication server.
tldr.outcome: ERP enables fast handovers and was designed to support efficient roaming in mobile networks. It was later superseded by RFC 6696, which extends the approach.

today: RFC 5296 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 6696, which extends ERP with additional capabilities. RFC 6696 is the current standard for EAP re-authentication.

sections.title: The Problem with Full Re-authentication
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) is a framework that supports many types of authentication methods. When a device connects to a network, an EAP server and a peer device authenticate each other through an intermediary called the EAP authenticator, which is typically the access point or router. After successful authentication, both the server and the peer hold keying material used for the security session.

When a device moves from one access point to another, it needs to re-authenticate. A full EAP exchange can involve multiple round trips and significant time to complete, causing delays in handover. Some EAP methods reduce this overhead through state reuse, but most require at least 2 round trips back to the original EAP server. ERP is designed to solve this with a faster, method-independent approach.
sections.eli5: Logging in to a network from scratch takes time because the server has to ask lots of questions. ERP lets you prove you are already logged in without asking all the questions again.

sections.title: The ERP Approach
sections.content:
ERP allows a peer and server to mutually verify that the peer still holds valid keying material from a previous full EAP authentication, then complete the re-authentication in a single round trip. The key insight is that the peer and server derive a re-authentication root key (rRK) from keying material already established during the initial EAP exchange. This rRK is kept secret between the peer and the server only and is never given to any other entity.

From the rRK, two more keys are derived: a re-authentication integrity key (rIK) used to protect the exchange, and a re-authentication MSK (rMSK) used as the session key for the new authenticator. The ER server can be located in the home domain (the original network) or in the local domain (the visited network) if a local ER server is available. The peer signals which domain's server it is contacting through a named NAI (network access identifier).
sections.eli5: During the first login, the server and device both write down a secret code. Later, the device shows the code to prove it is the same device, and the server gives it a new session key for the new network. The code is never shown to anyone else.

sections.title: Protocol Messages
sections.content:
ERP uses three main message types. The EAP-Initiate/Re-auth-Start message is optional and sent by the new authenticator to signal that it supports ERP. The EAP-Initiate/Re-auth message is sent by the peer to request re-authentication; it includes the keyName-NAI to identify the domain and the re-authentication server, a sequence number for replay protection, a cryptosuite indicating which integrity algorithm to use, and an authentication tag computed over the message using the rIK.

In response, the EAP-Finish/Re-auth message is sent by the server; it contains the same sequence number, a matching authentication tag proving the server holds the correct rIK, and optionally the key lifetimes and domain name (in a bootstrapping scenario). The authenticator forwards the rMSK from this message to the peer, which then uses it to establish the security association with the new authenticator.
sections.eli5: The device sends a message with its secret code and asks to log in. The server checks the code and sends back a new session key. The sequence number ensures the messages are fresh and not replayed.

sections.title: Key Hierarchy and Derivation
sections.content:
The rRK is derived from either the EMSK (Extended Master Session Key) from the original EAP exchange or from a domain-specific root key (DSRK) if the local ER server is in a different domain. The derivation uses a pseudorandom function and labeled input. The rRK length equals the parent key length and is never used directly to protect data; it is only used to derive the rIK and rMSK.

The rIK is derived from the rRK using the cryptosuite and key length as input, ensuring that different rIKs for different algorithms are cryptographically distinct even if derived from the same rRK. The rMSK is derived on demand for each re-authentication, using the sequence number from the peer's request as additional input, ensuring a unique session key for each authenticator. Both the rRK and rIK are never transported to any other entity; they remain only on the peer and the server.
sections.eli5: The secret code is stored safely and never sent anywhere. Two shorter codes are made from it: one for checking that the message is real, and one for the new network session. Each new network gets a different session code, even if they use the same secret.

sections.title: Security Properties
sections.content:
ERP provides mutual authentication: both the peer and server must possess the correct rRK to successfully complete the exchange. Sequence numbers prevent replay attacks. The rMSK is scoped to a single authenticator; no other authenticator can use it. Compromise of one rMSK does not compromise other rMSKs because each one is derived independently with a different sequence number.

One limitation is the lack of forward secrecy: if the rRK or DSRK is compromised, all past and future ERP exchanges using that key are compromised retroactively. Additionally, if the DSRK is delivered to a local ER server via AAA protocols, the AAA path can become a point of vulnerability. The specification recommends protecting AAA transport with IPsec or TLS, and the home server must not hand out a DSRK to a local domain more than once without verification that the recipient is the same entity.
sections.eli5: Both sides must prove they know the secret code. The order of messages is checked so the same message cannot be used twice. Each network gets its own session code so losing one session key does not break others. If someone steals the secret code, they can see all old and new sessions.
